extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, examiners, students, and interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the legal requirements that a patent application disclose an invention in sufficient detail (enablement/written description) so a person skilled in the art can carry it out, with jurisdictional notes (EPC, US) and special rules for biological materials and best mode. Useful for patent drafting, examination, opposition, and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must disclose a claimed invention in sufficient detail so that the person skilled in the art could carry out that claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is fundamental to patent law: a monopoly is granted in exchange for a disclosure of how to make or practice the invention. If a patent fails to contain such information, the patent is unenforceable or can be revoked. Inventors who do not want to teach the world may use trade secrets instead, but without an enabling patent they cannot stop competitors who independently develop the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC Article 83: disclosure must be clear and complete for a skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the European Patent Convention (Article 83), an application must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency is considered during examination and non-compliance is a ground for opposition (Article 100(b) EPC) and revocation (Article 138(1)(b) EPC). Example anti-pattern: citing standardisation documents for essential aspects without sufficient precision so that the skilled person would have to make 'undue efforts to find and get together the information' needed to carry out the invention. Insufficiency is also a ground for revocation under Section 72 of the UK Patents Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: US statutory requirement: 35 U.S.C. §112 — written description and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The US patent specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it, 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US law has been interpreted to contain two related but distinct requirements: written description and enablement. Written description justifies and supports the scope/terminology of the claims; enablement teaches how to make and use the invention. The two serve different purposes and are applied separately in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: ability to practice without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure 'enables' the invention if it allows a person of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents fail this test if they claim more than they teach (e.g., claiming all light bulbs but explaining only how to make one kind). A non-enabling claim may be rejected during examination or invalidated later. Enablement is evaluated as of the filing date, and patent owners cannot rely on experiments conducted post-application to establish enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue experimentation and the Wands factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Undue experimentation is the standard for failing enablement; it concerns unpredictability of outcome rather than merely quantity of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit (In re Wands) identified eight factors to consider: (1) the quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) the amount of direction or guidance presented; (3) the presence or absence of working examples; (4) the nature of the invention; (5) the state of the prior art; (6) the relative skill of those in the art; (7) the predictability or unpredictability of the art; and (8) the breadth of the claims. Predictable arts (mechanical, software) typically require little description (e.g., flow charts may suffice); unpredictable arts (chemistry, pharmaceuticals) require very detailed disclosure. Case examples: patents invalidated where specification did not enable PHOSITA without undue experimentation (e.g., some Lemelson patents). The Supreme Court (Amgen v. Sanofi) said the specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description / possession requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement demands that the applicant's disclosure demonstrate possession of the invention and sufficiently support the claims, preventing speculative filings for inventions not yet actually invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to prevent applicants from obtaining priority for inventions they have not yet invented. A written description deficiency can render claims invalid (example: University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle — claims to identifying inhibitors were invalid because no specific compounds were disclosed). Written description determines claim scope and prevents later asserting invention not described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit of biological material as a means to meet disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For biological materials that cannot be precisely described (e.g., cell lines, plasmids), making a deposit of the claimed material (e.g., under the Budapest Treaty) can be used to satisfy written description/enablement requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the US biological deposits may be made any time before patent issuance (and sometimes during reexamination), while many other countries require deposits before filing. Deposits are typically kept for around 30 years. The deposit option addresses difficulties in describing self-replicating biological materials where molecular structure is not available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure must contain the inventor's 'best mode' of making or practicing the invention (i.e., the preferred way known to the inventor at filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if the inventor knows the liquid should be heated to 250°C but only discloses 'above 200°C', the best mode was not disclosed. The best mode must be disclosed for the entire invention, not only its innovative aspects, and it applies to what the inventor knew at filing. Post-AIA US law no longer permits invalidation of a patent for failure to disclose the best mode, though the statutory language still mentions it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and evidentiary timing: enablement evaluated at filing date; written description treated differently
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is determined as of the filing date of the patent application; written description is a factual inquiry tied to the disclosure and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because enablement is fixed at filing date, post-filing experiments generally cannot cure an enabling deficiency. US courts treat enablement as a question of law based on underlying factual findings, whereas the written description requirement is often treated as a question of fact (sometimes decided by a jury). These procedural distinctions affect litigation and invalidity defenses.
